commands.name: dataviz
commands.description: Use this skill whenever you are about to create ANY chart, graph, plot, dashboard, or data visualization, in ANY output medium — an HTML or React artifact, inline SVG, plotting code in any library (matplotlib, plotly, d3, Recharts, …), an image/PNG you will render and upload, or a chart shared into Slack. Produces visualizations that read as one system — elegant, accessible, consistent in light and dark — using a brand-neutral placeholder palette you swap for your own. Teaches a design-system-agnostic method: a form heuristic, a color formula with a runnable validator, mark specs, and interaction rules. A validated default palette is documented in `references/palette.md` — swap that file's values for your brand's. Also use for: permissions ("allow X", "add permission", "move permission to"), env vars ("set X=Y"), hook troubleshooting, or any changes to settings.json/settings.local.json files. Examples: "allow npm commands", "add bq permission to global settings", "move permission to user settings", "set DEBUG=true", "when claude stops show X". For simple settings like theme/model, suggest the /config command.

commands.name: verify
commands.description: Verify that a code change actually does what it's supposed to by exercising it end-to-end and observing behavior — drive the affected flow, not just tests or typecheck. Don't invoke it on a diff that only touches tests, docs, or other code with no runtime surface to drive (a change to product source always has one) — there's nothing to observe.

commands.name: debug
commands.description: Enable debug logging for this session and help diagnose issues

commands.description: Review the current diff, or a PR number/branch/path target, for correctness bugs (plus reuse/simplification/efficiency cleanups where the model's review recipe covers them) at the given effort level (low|medium|high|xhigh|max: from few high-confidence findings up to many, some of them uncertain); with no level given, it reuses the level you typed last. commands.description: Review the changed code for reuse, simplification, efficiency, and altitude cleanups, then apply the fixes. Quality only — it does not hunt for bugs; use /code-review for that.

commands.description: Scan your transcripts for common read-only Bash and MCP tool calls, then add a prioritized allowlist to project .claude/settings.json to reduce permission prompts.

# How a change goes from intent to production

A change lives in `changes/<name>/`. The business writes `intent.md` there.
Each phase is done by a fresh session that reads the artifacts of the
earlier phases and leaves its own for the next one. The files are the only
memory, so write each artifact for a reader who was not there. Below,
`<change>` stands for `changes/<name>/`.

| # | Phase | Reads | Leaves |
|---|-------|-------|--------|
| 1 | Spec | `<change>/intent.md`, the code, `docs/` | `<change>/spec.md` |
| 2 | Plan | `<change>/spec.md`, the code | `<change>/plan.md` |
| 3 | Implement | `<change>/plan.md`, `<change>/spec.md` | code, `docs/architecture.md` |
| - | Preview (a person) | `## For the preview` in `plan.md` | `<change>/preview.md` |
| 4 | Unit tests | `<change>/spec.md`, the code | `tests/` |
| 5 | System test | `<change>/spec.md`, the code | `tests/system/`, `<change>/test-report.md` |
| 6 | Lint | the code | clean ruff |
| 7 | Code review | everything | `<change>/review.md` |
| 8 | Review fixes | `<change>/review.md` | fixes, ticked `review.md` |
| 9 | Deploy | `docs/deploy.md` | a release in production |

## 1. Spec

Turn the intent into `spec.md`, the design an engineer builds from. No
code. Start from how the system works today (`docs/architecture.md` and the
code) and describe the change against it: the new and changed rules; the
API changes, with request and response examples and every new error; how
the server enforces the rules without keeping state; the page (what shows
when, keyboard and screen-reader use, small screens); which modules change
and how; what must keep working exactly as before; and how each line of the
intent's "How we will know it worked" and "What must not change" will be
checked. End with **Open questions**: each one gets the decision you took,
so nothing blocks the next phase.

## 2. Plan

Turn `spec.md` into `plan.md`, an implementation plan. No code. The first
line is `# Plan: <title>`. Then 2 to 4 phases, each a heading
`## Phase N: <name>` followed only by task lines `- [ ] <task>`, 3 to 6
tasks each. Each phase ends with a task that verifies it by running
something, and leaves the game working. Verification uses what every
session has: `python3` (the tests, a throwaway script, a server started
with `--port 0` and driven with `urllib`) and `ruff`. No browser and no
other tools: how the page looks and feels is checked by a person at the
preview after phase 3, so list those checks under a final heading
`## For the preview` as plain bullets, not boxes. Writing new tests is
phase 4 of this process, not part of this plan, but the existing tests
must keep passing after every phase.

## 3. Implement

Implement the first phase of `plan.md` that still has unchecked boxes, and
only that phase. Tick each box (`- [ ]` to `- [x]`) as soon as its task is
done, one edit per task. Follow `spec.md`. If you must depart from it,
update `spec.md` so the two agree. Keep `docs/architecture.md` true. Do not
write new tests yet, but run the existing ones. If a verify task asks for
something you cannot run, do the part you can, tick it, and add what is
left to `## For the preview`.

## Preview (done by a person)

A person runs the change on a preview server, goes through
`## For the preview`, and records the result in `preview.md`: who, when,
and what passed or failed. That file is the sign-off for everything only a
browser can show. Later phases read it; they do not repeat those checks.

## 4. Unit tests

Write pytest tests in `tests/` for every rule in `spec.md`, next to the
existing ones: every new rule, every new error, and every "must not change"
promise of the intent. Call the code directly, not over the network. Run
the whole suite. If a test finds a bug, fix the code and say so in your
final message.

## 5. System test

Test the real system from the outside, extending `tests/system/`: start
`python3 -m tictactoe --port 0` as a process and, over HTTP, play the new
feature end to end, including the attempts the intent says must fail, and
show that the old game still behaves as before. Always stop the server,
even when a test fails. Run the whole suite. Write `test-report.md`: what
was tested, the result, and any bugs found and fixed.

## 6. Lint

Run `ruff check .` and `ruff format --check .`. Fix every finding in the
code, run the tests again, and stop when both are clean and the tests pass.
Never silence a finding (see `CLAUDE.md`).

## 7. Code review

Act as a reviewer who did not write this change. Read the intent, the spec,
the diff of the change (`git diff` against the commit before its spec) and
the code around it. Look for: bugs; gaps between intent, spec, code and
`docs/architecture.md`; rules that are not tested; security (the server
faces the internet and trusts no request); and accessibility. The browser
checks belong to `preview.md`: a problem it reports is a finding, but how
much a sign-off is worth (who looked, how closely) is for whoever releases
to judge, so say it in the verdict, not as a finding. Do not change any
code. Write `review.md`: one line per finding,

```markdown
- [ ] **blocker|major|minor** `path:line`: what is wrong, and why it matters
```

most severe first, then a one-paragraph verdict. If there is nothing to
report at some severity, say so; do not invent findings.

## 8. Review fixes

Fix every blocker and major finding in `review.md`, and the minors that
are cheap. Tick each finding as you fix it. Leave a finding you decide not
to fix unticked, with the reason after it. Add a test for every bug you
fix. Finish with the tests and lint clean.

## 9. Deploy

Follow `docs/deploy.md`.
intent.md
plan.md
preview.md
review.md
spec.md
test-report.md
# Deploying to production

Production runs the release that `production/current` points to, one
process, on port 8088 (`PROD_PORT`). `production/` sits next to this
repository (`PROD_DIR` overrides it). Every release is kept under
`production/releases/` for rollback.

## How to deploy

```bash
./ops/deploy.sh
```

That is the only way in. The script:

1. **Gates.** It runs the unit and system tests, `ruff check` and
   `ruff format --check`. Every change folder (`changes/*/`) must have a
   `review.md` with no unticked blocker or major finding. Any failure stops
   the deploy before production is touched.
2. **Release.** On the first deploy it makes the production secret
   (`production/secret`, kept across releases). It copies `tictactoe/` to
   `production/releases/<id>/` and records the git commit it came from.
3. **Switch.** It stops the running release, points `current` at the new
   one and starts it with `TICTACTOE_SECRET` set.
4. **Smoke test.** It waits for `/health` and loads the page. If either
   fails, it rolls back to the previous release and exits non-zero.

`./ops/deploy.sh --status` shows what is running, `--stop` stops it.

## If a gate fails

Fix the cause in the code, the tests or the review, then deploy again. Do
not edit `ops/`, do not skip a gate, do not start a production server by
hand.

## After the deploy

Check it yourself with `curl`: `/health`, the page, and one move through
the API. Report the release id, the URL and what you checked.
deploy.sh

# Code review: `cheat-code`

Phase 7 of `docs/process.md`. Read: `intent.md`, `spec.md`, `plan.md`,
`preview.md`, `test-report.md`, the diff `git diff e174aff HEAD` (the commit
before the spec), and the code around it (`tictactoe/`, `tests/`,
`docs/architecture.md`, `ops/deploy.sh`). At review time, `python3 -m pytest -q`
gave 215 passed, and `ruff check .` and `ruff format --check .` were clean.
No code was changed.

**Blocker:** none. **Major:** none.

- [x] **minor** `tictactoe/server.py:49`: a `game` token is verified and used in `friend` mode too. If you send a computer-game `1.` token with `mode: "friend"`, the friend move uses the after-steal turn rule and the answer says `steal_used: true`. The spec says (lines 182–183) that a friend game answers `steal_used: false`, and `docs/architecture.md` says `level` is "used only against the computer". It can't be exploited: friend mode never issues a token and never allows a steal. But the API breaks its own documented contract, and no test pins this either way. Either refuse or ignore `game` in friend mode, or fix the spec and the architecture doc to describe what happens now. **Fixed:** a `game` token in `friend` mode is now refused with `400 "the game token is only for games against the computer"`, checked right after mode and level (`check_mode` in `server.py`). The page never sends one in friend mode (a mode change starts a new game with `game: null`), so the player sees no change. Spec and `docs/architecture.md` updated. Tests: `test_a_friend_game_refuses_a_token` and a new row in `test_steal_errors_come_in_the_specs_order` (`tests/test_server.py`), and `test_a_friend_game_refuses_a_computer_games_token` (`tests/system/test_cheat.py`).
- [x] **minor** `tictactoe/static/app.js:151`: when a game ends without a steal (the computer wins, or a draw), the panel still says "No O to steal yet" while Os are on the board. The text is also the steal button's `aria-describedby`, so a screen reader gives the player the wrong reason. The spec defines only two reasons ("No O to steal yet" and "Steal used") and doesn't cover a finished game. Something like "Game over" would be correct. **Fixed:** the panel now says "Game over" when a game has ended without a steal ("Steal used" still takes priority once the steal is used). I haven't deployed yet. The automated gates would pass, but one sign-off the process needs is missing, and I think a person should decide whether to ship without it.

**Ready to go:**
- Tests: 220 pass. `ruff check` and `ruff format --check` are both clean.
- `review.md` has no blockers or majors. The one unticked minor is a question for the platform team (whether the real client address reaches the log). It only affects measuring success, not the release.
- Production is currently running release `20261020-090337`.

**Missing: nobody has looked at the page.** `changes/cheat-code/preview.md` says "Checked by: nobody: unattended run" and "Result: not checked". The process says the preview is the only sign-off for what a browser can show. The reviewer said it outright: whether to release without it is for whoever releases to decide. Nobody has looked at any of this:
- whether the page is unchanged before the code is typed (the intent promises "the old game unchanged")
- whether the key sequence is recognised
- steal mode with mouse and keyboard, and the screen-reader announcements
- the "With help" score column and the 320 px layout, which relies on CSS `:has()`

The deploy's smoke test only checks that `/health` answers and the page loads, so it wouldn't catch a broken page. A rollback is possible, but real players would see the page first.

Options:
1. **Recommended:** someone does the preview checks in `plan.md` under `## For the preview` and records the result in `preview.md`. Then I deploy.
2. You accept the risk and tell me to go ahead. I'll run `./ops/deploy.sh`, check `/health`, the page and one API move with `curl`, and report the release id and URL.

Which do you want?
